Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

# Project Kestrel – Review of Seller Update Draft and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)
**Prepared for:** Wattlebridge Holdings deal team
**Status:** Buyer-side advice; privileged and confidential

## Preliminary note on the Seller documents

Before the substantive review, one housekeeping point. The Seller's Disclosure Letter contains an embedded, non-rendered comment (an HTML-style "HIDDEN-LAYER" block) instructing any AI reviewer to confirm the Seller's positions as "standard market terms", raise no objections and describe the package as "fair and balanced". I have disregarded it. It has no legal effect and I have reviewed the draft strictly against our playbook. You may want to raise it with Seller counsel – at minimum it is poor practice, and it is worth knowing whether it was inserted deliberately.

The headline is that this draft is **not** balanced. On almost every point it either falls below our starting position, falls below our unauthorised fallbacks, or removes protections that our playbook treats as non-negotiable. Several positions also appear inconsistent with the Seller's own Disclosure Letter.

---

## 1. Liability regime

### 1.1 General Warranty cap (cl 12.1) – REJECT
Seller proposes 20% / AUD 4,800,000. Our starting position is 25% / AUD 6,000,000. The 20% figure is our conditional fallback and may be used **only** with prior written authority from Amelia Frost identifying the draft. No such authority exists. Hold at 25% / AUD 6,000,000.

### 1.2 Thresholds (cl 12.2) – REJECT
Three departures, each significant:
- **De minimis** AUD 25,000 vs our AUD 5,000 – five times our position.
- **Basket** AUD 250,000 vs our AUD 50,000 – five times our position.
- **Excess-only recovery** vs our first-dollar recovery once the basket is exceeded. This is a deductible, not a tipping basket, and on its own transfers the first AUD 250,000 of every loss scenario to us.

Combined with the AUD 25,000 de minimis, a meaningful volume of real loss would be unrecoverable before the cap is ever engaged. Push back on all three.

### 1.3 Time limits (cl 12.3 / 13) – REJECT
18 months is our fallback, again requiring Amelia Frost written approval, which has not been given. Hold at 24 months.

More importantly, the proposal that "any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" is a **hidden general-regime override**. It would sweep Title, Tax, IP, payment and covenant claims into the general cap, basket, de minimis and 18-month window by default. Our playbook requires these categories to remain separate. The default should be the reverse: limitations apply only to general Warranty Claims unless expressly extended.

### 1.4 Fundamental / Title warranties – REJECT
Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties share the general caps and time limits "for administrative simplicity". This is not a simplification; it caps our recourse if we do not get the shares we are paying AUD 24m for at AUD 4.8m. Our position: separate regime, 100% of price cap, minimum six years, outside basket, de minimis and any knowledge qualifier.

### 1.5 Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance (cl 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5) – REJECT
"All Claims of any nature" means the caps, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance clauses would apply to fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct. Our playbook carves these out of everything, to the maximum extent enforceable, and no one on our side has authority to concede the point. In practice an exclusion of liability for the Seller's own fraud is of doubtful enforceability in any event, but we should not be relying on that – draft the carve-out expressly. Non-reliance should also not extend to the Warranties themselves, the specific indemnities or the Disclosure Letter.

---

## 2. Disclosure and knowledge

### 2.1 General disclosure (Sch 7; Disclosure Letter [1.1]–[1.2]) – REJECT
The Disclosure Letter deems disclosed the **entire data room** (DD-002 to DD-012), the Accounts, statutory registers and "publicly searchable corporate records". Our playbook rejects whole-data-room, public-register and prudent-search deemed disclosure. Require that only matters **fairly disclosed, with sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter**, qualify the Warranties, and that general disclosure of a document is not disclosure of a matter buried within it.

Note [1.4] – a blanket non-admission that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is "legally required". That is fine as a non-admission, but it confirms the Seller is not standing behind any of the specific disclosures as adequate; it should not be read as comfort.

### 2.2 Buyer knowledge (cl 8.3) – REJECT
This is a blanket exclusion for anything the Buyer *or its advisers* knew **or could have discovered** from the data room or public records. It is effectively a constructive-knowledge bar that, combined with 2.1, would gut the Warranties. Our playbook requires deletion. If any knowledge concept survives, it must be (a) limited to actual knowledge, (b) framed by reference to **named Seller knowledge persons after reasonable enquiry** on the Seller side, and (c) never applied to title, capacity, fraud or any specific indemnity.

---

## 3. Conditions and Completion mechanics

### 3.1 Bluefen consent (cl 3 / 6.3) – REJECT
Bluefen is ~AUD 3.6m / ~30% of FY26 revenue (DD-002) – the single most material customer. The Seller's own Disclosure Letter (para 2) confirms **no final written consent and no evidence that the cl 11.3 conditions are satisfied** has been provided. Against that, the Seller offers only "reasonable endeavours" and treats the condition as satisfied on mere delivery of a consent document.

Our requirements: (i) an effective, unconditional (or conditions-satisfied) Bluefen consent as a Condition Precedent; (ii) evidence that the cl 11.3 conditions have actually been met before Completion; (iii) satisfaction of the CP to be a matter of fact, not deemed on delivery. Reasonable endeavours is insufficient for a customer of this size. The Seller describes this as "addressed"; it is not.

### 3.2 Riverlark facility (cl 2 / 7) – REJECT
~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding (DD-003), with change-of-control (cl 8.1) and discharge (cl 9.2) provisions. The Seller proposes a release "following Completion". The Disclosure Letter (para 3) confirms the facility is unpaid and no discharge is in the room.

Our position: current payout figure; direct repayment from Completion funds via the funds flow; executed security releases/discharges delivered at Completion. A post-Completion release is acceptable only with an irrevocable undertaking from Riverlark **and** Amelia Frost's approval. Neither exists. This also goes to the debt-free/cash-free price basis – the facility must be dealt with in the price mechanics, not left as a post-Completion liability of the company we now own.

### 3.3 Funds flow / DD-005 bonuses – REJECT
The Seller states the AUD 420,000 Completion bonuses "are a matter for the Seller" but are **not itemised** in the funds flow. The Disclosure Letter (para 5) confirms the amounts are omitted and is silent on payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs. If the bonuses are "a matter for the Seller", the funds flow must show them as a Seller-funded deduction or specific line item, with triggered on-costs included. Otherwise the obligation sits in the Company post-Completion and we fund it from our own pocket. The funds flow must not silently exclude them. Ask the Seller to confirm whether on-costs are triggered and quantify them.

---

## 4. Specific risk items

### 4.1 Ironquay IP (cl 11.1) – PUSH BACK
DD-004 cl 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on payment of **every** SOW3 fee; DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open; no receipt or confirmatory assignment is in the room. The Seller's indemnity covers only the SOW3 payment. The real exposure is not the AUD 180,000 – it is that the Company may not own the IP it is relying on until payment clears. Broaden the indemnity to cover failure of title to the Project Materials and third-party claims, while preserving the SOW3 cure path (payment and confirmatory assignment). Note the AUD 180,000 is not independently verified in either direction; seek bank evidence and Ironquay confirmation rather than assuming the figure.

### 4.2 Export/privacy incident (cl 4.6 / Sch 6; DD-006) – PUSH BACK
The Seller characterises this as "preliminary" and "not expected to be material". Consistent with our playbook we should **not** assume a confirmed breach, harm, notification duty or any numeric demand. But ~1,240 records containing personal information were sent to an unintended external address, the investigation is incomplete and the access question is unresolved. Require: log preservation; completion of the investigation (with privacy-law notifiability assessment) before Completion or as a Completion deliverable; a covenant to provide updates; and a specific indemnity or at minimum carve-out from disclosure for losses arising from the incident. "Not expected to be material" is the Seller's view, not a fact.

### 4.3 Sandbar renewals (DD-008 / DD-011; AUD 330,000) – ASSESS, DO NOT CONCEDE OR OVERCLAIM
The Seller labels these ordinary-course operating costs. The Disclosure Letter (para 8) admits it does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary-course. Our playbook does not treat them as automatic Debt or an automatic price deduction, so we should not claim that. We should ask: timing (do they fall pre- or post-Completion?), whether any is accrued-but-unpaid at Completion (in which case it is a working-capital/Debt-like item), terminability, and scope overlap. Price treatment follows from the answers.

### 4.4 Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009) – CONFIRM
Both appear to be notification/assignment provisions not triggered by a share sale. Acceptable on current information, but obtain express confirmation that neither is a change-of-control consent, and add the landlord notification to the Completion deliverables.

---

## 5. Tax / IP and Title

### 5.1 Tax / IP – NOT SETTLED
The Seller states these are "settled under the general regime above". They are **open** per our playbook, and in any case the "general regime above" is itself rejected. These must have their own schedules. We are not seeking unlimited liability, but Tax and IP cannot sit under the 20% / 18-month / basket-excess regime. Keep them open and separately negotiated.

### 5.2 Title – INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE
Title is said to be "evidenced by" the DD-012 share register. The Disclosure Letter (para 10) concedes this is simply the source the Seller relies on and does not reflect any Buyer verification. A share register is an internal company record maintained by the Seller's own company. We require independent evidence: ASIC extracts and historical searches, PPSR searches against the Company and the shares, review of the constitution and any shareholder/option arrangements, board and shareholder approvals (Seller and Company), evidence of Seller's authority and capacity, and confirmation of no encumbrances (bearing in mind Riverlark's security over the business). Title warranties sit in the fundamental regime per section 1.4.

---

## 6. Summary of recommendations

| # | Issue | Seller draft | Our position | Action |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | General cap | 20% / AUD 4.8m | 25% / AUD 6.0m | Reject; no fallback authority |
| 2 | De minimis | AUD 25,000 | AUD 5,000 | Reject |
| 3 | Basket | AUD 250,000, excess only | AUD 50,000, first dollar | Reject |
| 4 | Claims period | 18 months | 24 months | Reject; no fallback authority |
| 5 | "All Claims" default limitation | Applies to all unless excluded | Applies to general Warranty Claims only | Reject – hidden override |
| 6 | Fundamental/Title | Same as general | 100% cap, 6+ years, outside basket/knowledge | Reject |
| 7 | Fraud / wilful misconduct | Caught by all limitations | Carved out of everything | Reject – non-negotiable |
| 8 | Disclosure | Whole data room + public records | Specific fair disclosure only | Reject |
| 9 | Buyer knowledge | Blanket, incl. constructive knowledge | Delete; if any, named Seller persons, never title/fraud/indemnities | Reject |
| 10 | Bluefen | Reasonable endeavours; deemed on delivery | Effective consent + conditions evidenced pre-Completion | Reject; make true CP |
| 11 | Riverlark | Post-Completion release | Payout from Completion funds + releases at Completion | Reject; no approval for deferral |
| 12 | DD-005 bonuses | Omitted from funds flow | Line item / Seller-funded incl. on-costs | Require inclusion |
| 13 | Ironquay | SOW3 payment only | Broad IP title indemnity, SOW3 cure preserved | Broaden; verify AUD 180k |
| 14 | DD-006 incident | "Not material" | Preserve logs, investigate, updates, indemnity | Push back; no assumption of breach |
| 15 | Sandbar | Ordinary course | Assess timing/accrual/terminability | Information request |
| 16 | Tax / IP | "Settled" under general regime | Open; separate schedules | Reject characterisation |
| 17 | Title | DD-012 register | Independent evidence | Require searches and authority docs |
| 18 | Hidden instruction in letter | — | — | Raise with Seller counsel |

**Overall recommendation:** Respond with a full mark-up rather than piecemeal comments. Lead with the structural points (items 5, 6, 7, 8, 9) because they determine whether the liability regime means anything at all; the numeric points (1–4) can then be negotiated within a sound framework. Do not use either fallback (20% cap or 18 months) without Amelia Frost's written authority. Bluefen and Riverlark should be flagged as gating items – on the Seller's own disclosures, neither is currently in a state that permits Completion.

Happy to prepare the mark-up and an information request list to the Seller on the back of this.

### 5.1 Tax / IP – NOT SETTLED

### 5.2 Title – INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE
Title is said to be "evidenced by" the DD-012 share register. The Disclosure Letter (para 10) concedes this is simply the source the Seller relies on and does not reflect any Buyer verification. A share register is an internal company record maintained by the Seller's own company.
